To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) WHO feeding indicators (FIS) are associated with stunting and with underweight in low-income countries; (2) FIS were not associated with country-level gross national income (GN); (3) FIS were associated with maternal education; and (4) FIS were significantly associated with reduced risk of underweight, stunting and undernutrition in low-income countries.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship of child growth to feeding practices and to the quality of the child's diet.
the relationship between the World Health Organization infant and young child (WHO) feeding indicator and growth in 14 low income countries.
the relationship between infant and young child nutrition and growth in 14 low income countries in Asia, Africa, and Latin America.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
early initiation of breastfeeding, introduction of complementary foods at six months and continued breastfeeding at 2 years of age are all associated with reduced risk of underweight.
the World Health Organization feeding indicators are useful for assessing the feeding practices of children in developing countries.

the feeding of infants and children under 24 months of age with a minimum acceptable diet (including a minimum frequency and a minimum number of food groups) is associated with lower prevalence of stunting and undernutrition.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

early breastfeeding and complementary feeding with solid foods are associated with a lower risk of stunting and undernutrition, while continued breastfeeding at 6-23 months is associated with a higher risk of stunting, underweight and wasting.
early introduction of solids and meeting WHO guidance for dietary diversity, minimum acceptable diet, and IRF are associated with reduced risk of underweight.

the feeding indicators that were most associated with growth measures were those that reflected the introduction of complementary foods at the appropriate time, the consumption of foods that were rich in iron, and the consumption of a diverse diet.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the World Health Organization (W.H.O.) indicators are not all associated with growth and that some of the associations are in the opposite direction to what is expected.
feeding indicators are associated with growth in poor countries and that maternal education is a variable associated with feeding indicators and child growth.
the WHO feeding indicators (F1-F8) are associated with child growth outcomes in low-income countries.
